title: Release data
text:
Portable export
Programmatically, a complete project can be exported with:
export_dir <- export_protvis_dataset(
  dataset,
  directory = "ProtVis_release",
  include_raw = FALSE
)
The export contains ProtVis_dataset.rds, expression/sample/protein tables, annotation files, process history, stored analysis results, metadata JSON, and an HTML report. Set include_raw = TRUE when attached input files should also be copied and licensing/privacy rules permit it.

title: Release data
text:
Manuscript-ready package
For a publication, keep a simple hierarchy such as:
ProtVis_release/
  data/
  metadata/
  statistics/
  enrichment/
  figures/
  methods/
  ProtVis_dataset.rds
Do not use screenshots as the only copy of a quantitative result. Export the table behind every key figure.






Tip



Record the ProtVis package version and the date of the final analysis. For actively developed software, a commit SHA or tagged release improves reproducibility further.

title: RAW → mzML with MSConvert
text:
ProtVis’s Raw workflow currently starts from .mzML + FASTA, whereas many mass spectrometers produce vendor-specific raw files such as Thermo Scientific .raw. Before Project init → Raw and Search (Sage), convert the vendor files to the open mzML format.
For Windows users, the recommended route is ProteoWizard MSConvert. ProteoWizard provides both the graphical MSConvertGUI application and the command-line msconvert.exe utility.
The complete route is:
Vendor RAW → ProteoWizard/MSConvert → mzML → ProtVis Project init → Sage Search → ProtVis_dataset






ImportantVendor RAW conversion is best performed on Windows



ProteoWizard can read and write open formats across platforms, but reading most vendor-specific formats depends on vendor libraries. The official ProteoWizard documentation recommends Windows for direct vendor-format conversion. For the Thermo .raw files used by the ProtVis example, perform conversion on Windows before moving the resulting .mzML files to Windows, Linux, or macOS for downstream analysis.

title: RAW → mzML with MSConvert
text:
Download ProteoWizard / MSConvert
Use the official ProteoWizard download page:

ProteoWizard official download page
ProteoWizard user documentation
MSConvert documentation

On the download page:

Select the ProteoWizard binary distribution for Windows.
Prefer the current 64-bit Windows installer on a modern 64-bit Windows system.
Read and accept the required license agreements for bundled vendor readers.
Download the installer.

ProteoWizard is currently released as version 3.x, but the detailed build number changes frequently. For reproducibility, record the installed ProteoWizard/MSConvert version in your Methods or analysis notes rather than documenting only “MSConvert”.

title: RAW → mzML with MSConvert
text:
Install on Windows
Run the downloaded installer and keep the default components unless your local IT policy requires another location. The current ProteoWizard download page states that the Windows installer requires Microsoft .NET Framework 4.7.2 or newer.
After installation, Windows should provide the ProteoWizard tools, including:

MSConvertGUI — graphical conversion interface;
msconvert.exe — command-line converter;
other ProteoWizard utilities such as SeeMS.

A typical installation is under a versioned ProteoWizard directory inside C:\Program Files\ProteoWizard\, although the exact path depends on the installed build. If several ProteoWizard versions are present, use the newest validated version consistently for a project.

Confirm the installation
Open Command Prompt or PowerShell, navigate to the ProteoWizard installation directory if necessary, and run:
msconvert.exe --help
If Windows cannot find msconvert.exe, either run it with its full path or add the ProteoWizard installation directory to your PATH.
You can also confirm the graphical installation by searching the Start menu for MSConvert or MSConvertGUI.

title: RAW → mzML with MSConvert
text:
Recommended conversion with MSConvertGUI
For most ProtVis users, the graphical interface is the easiest route.

1. Start MSConvertGUI
Open MSConvertGUI from the Windows Start menu or from the ProteoWizard installation directory.


2. Add RAW files
Use Browse / Add to select one or more vendor RAW files. Batch conversion is recommended so that all samples are processed with exactly the same settings.
For the six-control-sample ProtVis example based on PXD065315, the source files are:
B73_C1.raw
B73_C2.raw
B73_C3.raw
EA2024_C1.raw
EA2024_C2.raw
EA2024_C3.raw


3. Select the output directory
Choose a clean output directory containing only the converted files for the current ProtVis project, for example:
E:\PXD065315\mzML\
Keeping vendor RAW and converted mzML in separate directories makes file validation and reproducibility easier.


4. Set the output format to mzML
Use:
Output format: mzML
mzML is ProteoWizard’s default open output format and is the format expected by the current ProtVis Raw/Sage workflow.


5. Use zlib compression
Enable zlib compression to reduce mzML file size without changing the underlying numerical spectra.
For general proteomics conversion, keep the default m/z precision unless you have a validated reason to reduce it. ProteoWizard currently defaults to 64-bit m/z encoding and 32-bit intensity encoding.


6. Add Peak Picking when the RAW file contains profile spectra
For profile-mode data that should be centroided before database search, add the Peak Picking filter and apply it to all MS levels:
peakPicking true 1-
When vendor centroiding is required, keep Peak Picking first in the filter list. ProteoWizard’s own msconvert documentation notes that vendor peak-picking algorithms operate on raw, untransformed data and therefore must be applied before other filters.
For typical Thermo proteomics RAW → Sage workflows, this is a practical default when the source data are profile-mode. If the instrument method already exported centroid spectra, do not apply redundant centroiding simply because the option exists.






WarningDo not add filters without a reason



Filters change the spectra passed to Sage. Avoid aggressive thresholding, scan removal, mass-window restriction, or other transformations unless they are part of a documented analysis plan. For a general ProtVis workflow, mzML output + zlib compression + appropriate centroiding is usually sufficient.




7. Start conversion
Click Start and wait until every file has completed without error.
The output should preserve the original filename stem:
B73_C1.raw     → B73_C1.mzML
B73_C2.raw     → B73_C2.mzML
EA2024_C1.raw  → EA2024_C1.mzML
This naming is important because ProtVis maps sample_info$mzml_file to the files in the selected mzML directory.

title: RAW → mzML with MSConvert
text:
Command-line conversion with msconvert.exe
The command-line utility is convenient for scripted or repeated conversions.

Convert one RAW file
msconvert.exe "E:\RAW\B73_C1.raw" --mzML --zlib --filter "peakPicking true 1-" -o "E:\mzML"


Convert all RAW files in a directory
msconvert.exe "E:\RAW\*.raw" --mzML --zlib --filter "peakPicking true 1-" -o "E:\mzML"
The important options are:







Option
Meaning




--mzML
write mzML output; mzML is also the current default


--zlib
compress binary arrays with zlib


--filter "peakPicking true 1-"
centroid spectra at MS1 and higher levels when appropriate


-o
set the output directory



For data that are already centroided, omit the peak-picking filter:
msconvert.exe "E:\RAW\*.raw" --mzML --zlib -o "E:\mzML"
To inspect the exact options supported by your installed build:
msconvert.exe --help
msconvert.exe --show-examples

Connect the mzML files to ProtVis
Once conversion is complete:

title: RAW → mzML with MSConvert
text:
Troubleshooting
MSConvert cannot open the vendor RAW file. Perform vendor-format conversion on Windows and confirm that you installed a ProteoWizard build with the required vendor readers. Do not assume a native Linux build can read proprietary vendor data.
The mzML files are extremely large. Confirm that zlib compression is enabled. If the source is profile-mode and your downstream search requires centroided spectra, confirm that Peak Picking was applied appropriately.
Sage finds no spectra or very few PSMs. First verify that the mzML contains valid MS1/MS2 spectra and that centroiding was appropriate. Then check the FASTA, precursor/fragment tolerances, enzyme, modifications, and acquisition type.
ProtVis reports missing mzML files. The filename in sample_info$mzml_file must match the converted file name exactly, including the .mzML extension.
The conversion works on one sample but fails on others. Inspect the MSConvert log for the failing files and confirm that all source files were completely downloaded/copied and were acquired using a vendor format supported by your installed ProteoWizard build.

title: RAW → mzML with MSConvert
text:
Reproducibility checklist
Record the following information with the project:
ProteoWizard/MSConvert version:
Operating system:
Original vendor format:
Output format: mzML
zlib compression: yes/no
Peak Picking: yes/no
Peak Picking MS levels:
Additional filters:
Conversion date:
Keeping these settings together with the original RAW files, converted mzML files, FASTA, Sage configuration, and ProtVis project directory makes the Raw → Sage workflow substantially easier to reproduce.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text: The STRINGdb PPI toolkit converts a biologically motivated candidate-gene list into a STRING protein-protein interaction network. It can be used after DEP analysis, enrichment, WGCNA, PTM analysis or any other workflow that produces a focused gene/protein set.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text: The STRINGdb PPI toolkit converts a biologically motivated candidate-gene list into a STRING protein-protein interaction network. It can be used after DEP analysis, enrichment, WGCNA, PTM analysis or any other workflow that produces a focused gene/protein set.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
STRINGdb PPI interface
The screenshot below shows the current STRINGdb PPI interface with demonstration data. The left sidebar is organized as a four-step workflow—Data Input, STRING Settings, Network Options, and Color & Export—while the main area summarizes mapping and network size and provides tabs for the network and the underlying data tables.






Figure 1: ProtVis STRINGdb PPI interface showing the four-step sidebar, summary cards and the protein-protein interaction network.



The counts and interaction pattern visible in the screenshot belong only to the bundled demonstration dataset; your network size will depend on the submitted identifiers, species, STRING version and confidence threshold.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
1. Data Input
ProtVis supports three input modes:

Demo data loads the bundled example gene table.
Upload file accepts CSV, TSV or text files.
Paste genes accepts a pasted gene list or table.

A gene-symbol column is required for mapping. A quantitative column such as log2FC is optional but useful because ProtVis can use it to color network nodes. After data are loaded, the module exposes column controls so the correct gene and fold-change columns can be selected.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
2. STRING Settings
Choose the STRING database version, species and confidence threshold before running the network analysis. The current interface provides STRING 11.5 and 12.0, with 11.5 selected by default.
Common organism presets include human, mouse, rat, Arabidopsis, rice, maize, soybean, tomato, Setaria viridis, yeast, fruit fly, C. elegans and E. coli K12. A Custom taxonomy ID option is also available when the target species is not in the preset list. The default interaction confidence threshold is 400, and an optional STRING cache directory can be supplied.






Important



Always verify the selected species before interpreting the network. A valid gene symbol can map to different proteins—or fail to map entirely—when the wrong taxonomy ID is used.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
3. Network Options
The network can be restricted to input proteins or allowed to include additional STRING-connected proteins depending on the Keep input proteins only setting. The Keep disconnected mapped proteins option allows successfully mapped candidates to remain visible even when they have no retained interaction edge.
Available layouts include Fruchterman-Reingold, Kamada-Kawai, Circle, and Stress. Node size can be scaled by degree or held at a user-defined default size, and label size can also be adjusted.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
4. Color and export
If a fold-change column is available, node color can represent the selected log2 fold-change range. The default color scale spans -2 to 2. Plot width and height are configurable, and the network can currently be downloaded as PDF or PNG.
The sidebar also provides Download Demo Data, which is useful for learning the expected input structure before preparing a custom dataset.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
Result tabs
After running the analysis, ProtVis organizes the output into several tabs:

Network — publication-oriented PPI visualization.
Input Preview — the table actually used for mapping.
Mapping — input identifiers and their mapped STRING protein IDs, with a downloadable mapping table.
Nodes — node-level information including gene symbol, optional log2FC and degree.
Edges — STRING interaction records and combined confidence scores.
Species Search — search supported STRING organisms and retrieve taxonomy IDs for custom species settings.

The summary cards above the tabs report the number of input genes, successfully mapped proteins, network size, STRING version and species ID, making it easier to identify mapping losses before interpreting the network.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
Recommended workflow

Prepare a clean gene/protein list and, when available, a quantitative column such as log2FC.
Confirm the correct species/taxonomy ID and STRING version.
Set an interaction-confidence threshold appropriate for the exploratory or publication context.
Run the analysis and inspect the mapping table before interpreting the network.
Review disconnected mapped proteins rather than silently treating them as failed candidates.
Adjust the network layout, labels and node scaling for readability.
Export the figure together with the mapping, node and edge tables used to generate it.

title: STRINGdb PPI
text:
Interpretation
STRING integrates evidence from multiple channels, including known and predicted associations. A STRING edge therefore does not necessarily mean direct physical binding in the biological system used in your experiment. Use the network to organize hypotheses and prioritize candidates, then support important interactions with literature, orthogonal databases or experimental validation.

title: Protein links
text:
Use Toolkits → Protein links when you want to move quickly from a gene/protein identifier or an amino-acid sequence to external protein resources. ProtVis supports two routes: a direct identifier lookup through the UniProt REST service, or a local BLASTP fallback against user-configured Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL databases.
After a UniProt accession has been resolved, ProtVis provides quick links to UniProt, InterPro, and the SWISS-MODEL Repository. This makes Protein Links the natural entry point for moving from an identifier to annotation and then to structure-oriented inspection.

title: Protein links
text:
Protein Links interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current interface using AT5G22800 as an example query. The right side illustrates the external annotation pages reached from the resolved protein entry. The Windows BLAST database and executable paths visible in the screenshot belong to that computer only and should not be copied literally to another machine.






Figure 1: ProtVis Protein Links interface showing direct gene-ID lookup, protein-sequence input, local Swiss-Prot/TrEMBL BLAST database paths, BLASTP executable configuration and linked external protein resources.

title: Protein links
section: Swiss-Model structure result from Protein Links
text:
Swiss-Model structure result from Protein Links
After the protein identity has been resolved, the structure-related link can be used to continue into Swiss-Model-oriented inspection. The screenshot below belongs in this Protein Links workflow because it illustrates the structure follow-up reached after protein identification and annotation rather than the initial identifier-mapping step itself.






Figure 2: Swiss-Model result view used as the structure follow-up in the Protein Links workflow. The protein sequence, project information, model-quality table and structure-analysis tabs are visible. The API-token value has been redacted for safe publication.



The structure view should be interpreted in the following order: first confirm the resolved protein and sequence; then inspect the returned Project Information and Model Quality; finally use PDB Information, Ramachandran Plot, Residue Composition, and 3D Structure to evaluate the model. If the structure is used in a figure or candidate-gene interpretation, record the model/project identifier and quality information together with the protein accession.






Important



Treat a Swiss-Model API token as a credential. Do not publish it in screenshots, manuscripts, repositories, or shared project files. The token field in the screenshot above has been redacted.

title: Protein links
section: Route 1: direct gene or protein identifier lookup
text:
Route 1: direct gene or protein identifier lookup
1. Enter a gene identifier or UniProt-compatible identifier. Type the identifier in Enter Gene ID or Protein Sequence. In the screenshot, the example is AT5G22800.
2. Let ProtVis query UniProt. For a non-empty identifier, the current implementation sends a UniProtKB search request and uses the first returned primary accession. No local BLAST database is required for this route.
3. Check the resolved protein before interpreting it. Open UniProt and verify the organism, gene/protein name, sequence length and functional annotation. In the screenshot, the example resolves to an Arabidopsis protein entry. The exact accession and annotation displayed are example-specific and should not be treated as expected output for another identifier.
4. Follow the Quick Links. Once a UniProt accession is available, ProtVis builds direct links to UniProt, InterPro, and SWISS-MODEL Repository. UniProt and InterPro may themselves expose additional links to resources such as AlphaFold or other structural/domain services, but these are external-site links rather than additional ProtVis mapping steps.

title: Protein links
text:
Route 2: sequence-based BLASTP fallback
Use this route when a stable identifier is unavailable or direct UniProt mapping does not resolve the protein.
1. Paste the amino-acid sequence. Enter the protein sequence in Enter protein sequence. Remove FASTA description text unless it is intentionally part of the sequence input.
2. Set the Swiss-Prot database path. SwissProt database path must point to a local BLAST-formatted Swiss-Prot protein database.
3. Set the TrEMBL database path. TrEMBL database path must point to a local BLAST-formatted TrEMBL protein database.
4. Set the BLASTP executable path. BLASTp executable path must point to the local NCBI BLAST+ blastp executable. For example, on Windows this is typically a path ending in blastp.exe.
5. Click Run BLASTP. ProtVis writes the sequence to a temporary FASTA file and runs BLASTP in XML output mode. The current search strategy queries Swiss-Prot first and only searches TrEMBL if no Swiss-Prot hit is returned.
6. Verify the mapped hit. The underlying BLAST helper retrieves the top hit and calculates sequence identity from the HSP identity count divided by aligned length. Treat this result as a candidate mapping that still requires biological review.
7. Use the resolved accession to open external resources. When a UniProt accession can be obtained, the same UniProt, InterPro and SWISS-MODEL quick links become available.

title: Protein links
text:
Local BLAST setup
The paths shown in the screenshot are examples from one Windows installation:
SwissProt database path: G:/blastdb/UniProt/uniprot_sprot
TrEMBL database path:    G:/blastdb/UniProt/uniprot_trembl
BLASTp executable path:  F:/NCBI/blast-2.17.0+/bin/blastp.exe
Replace all three with paths that exist on your own computer. The Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL databases must already be prepared in a BLAST-compatible format; entering the path to a downloaded FASTA file alone is not equivalent to providing a formatted BLAST database.

title: Protein links
section: How the current lookup priority works
text:
How the current lookup priority works
The current server logic follows this order:
Gene/protein identifier
        ↓
UniProt REST search
        ↓
first primary accession
        ↓
UniProt / InterPro / SWISS-MODEL links
If direct identifier mapping is unavailable and a protein sequence is supplied, ProtVis uses:
protein sequence
      ↓
Swiss-Prot BLASTP
      ↓ no hit
TrEMBL BLASTP
      ↓
resolved UniProt candidate






WarningVerify the biological identity



The first UniProt search result or the top BLAST hit is not automatically the correct ortholog, isoform, or functional counterpart. Check species, sequence coverage, identity, domain architecture and curated annotation before transferring biological interpretation.








ImportantDatabase paths are machine-specific



The G:/... and F:/... paths visible in the screenshot are demonstration paths from that Windows computer. They are not bundled with ProtVis and will not work unless the same local databases and BLAST+ installation exist at those locations.

title: DEG analyse
text:
Toolkits → DEG analyse is an RNA-seq-oriented utility and is separate from ProtVis’s main DEP analysis. The current implementation builds a DESeq2::DESeqDataSetFromMatrix, uses design = ~ Group, runs DESeq2::DESeq(), and produces PCA and volcano/result views.
Use this toolkit for raw count-style gene-expression data that are appropriate for DESeq2. Do not use it for normalized continuous proteomics intensities merely because proteins and RNA-seq both have samples in columns.

title: DEG analyse
text:
Toolkits → DEG analyse is an RNA-seq-oriented utility and is separate from ProtVis’s main DEP analysis. The current implementation builds a DESeq2::DESeqDataSetFromMatrix, uses design = ~ Group, runs DESeq2::DESeq(), and produces PCA and volcano/result views.
Use this toolkit for raw count-style gene-expression data that are appropriate for DESeq2. Do not use it for normalized continuous proteomics intensities merely because proteins and RNA-seq both have samples in columns.

title: DEG analyse
text:
DEG Analyse interface
The screenshot below shows a completed analysis with the PCA card on the left and the Volcano Plot card on the right. The displayed counts—4,559 up-regulated, 6,126 down-regulated and 10,685 significant features (19.48%)—belong to this particular uploaded example and are not fixed ProtVis results.






Figure 1: ProtVis DEG Analyse interface showing expression and group-file upload, PCA settings, volcano settings, PCA result and differential-expression volcano plot.

title: DEG analyse
text:
Required files
The current module accepts Excel .xlsx files for both inputs.
The Gene Expression Data workbook must contain an exact first-column identifier named:
GeneID
The remaining columns are sample count columns. The Group Information workbook must contain at least:
Sample
Group
Sample names must correspond to the expression-matrix sample columns because ProtVis reorders the count matrix using the row names created from the Sample field.

title: DEG analyse
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Upload Gene Expression Data. Select the count-matrix .xlsx. Keep genes in rows and samples in columns. The first column must be named exactly GeneID.
2. Upload Group Information. Select the grouping .xlsx. The first required field is Sample and the second is Group. Additional grouping columns can also be present and may become available for PCA color/shape mappings.
3. Verify that the data are raw counts. Before running, confirm that sample columns represent non-negative count data appropriate for DESeq2. In the current implementation ProtVis applies ceiling() to all sample values before constructing the DESeq2 count matrix; this is not a justification for supplying normalized continuous expression values.
4. Be aware of the current contrast. The present dev implementation extracts differential results with:
Group: B73 versus Y12
specifically contrast = c("Group", "B73", "Y12"). Therefore the current toolkit expects the Group column to contain the B73 and Y12 levels for differential testing. If your biological comparison uses different group names, this utility should not be treated as a generic arbitrary-group DEG interface without changing the underlying implementation.
5. Configure PCA Settings. Choose Color by and optionally Shape by from available grouping fields. Point size can be Small, Medium or Large. When grouping is used, ProtVis provides per-group color selectors. You can also show sample labels, encircle groups and display confidence ellipses; ellipse transparency and legend text size are configurable.
6. Configure Volcano Plot Settings. Set colors for Up-regulated, Down-regulated, and Not Significant points, point size, transparency, and grid display. These controls alter presentation only; they do not change the DEG classification threshold in the current implementation.
7. Click Run Analysis. ProtVis converts GeneID to row names, applies ceiling() to sample counts, aligns columns to the group-information sample order, creates a DESeq2 dataset with design = ~ Group, runs DESeq2, and extracts the B73-versus-Y12 result.
8. Inspect PCA Analysis. The Plot tab shows sample separation in principal-component space. Use PCA Data to inspect/export the coordinates rather than relying only on the figure. The percentage of variation displayed on PC1/PC2 is dataset-specific.
9. Inspect the Volcano Plot and DEG tables. The Plot tab displays fold change against significance. DEG Results exposes the underlying DESeq2 result table, while Statistics provides summary counts and top DEG information.
10. Export the analysis outputs. PCA settings provide PDF and PCA-data downloads. Volcano settings provide PDF and DEG-data downloads. The PCA and DEG table tabs also include CSV export controls.

title: DEG analyse
text:
Current DEG classification rule
The current implementation classifies a gene as Up-regulated when:
adjusted p-value < 0.05
and log2FoldChange > 1
and as Down-regulated when:
adjusted p-value < 0.05
and log2FoldChange < -1
All other genes are labeled Not significant. In other words, the current significance rule is padj < 0.05 together with |log2FoldChange| > 1.

title: DEG analyse
text:
PCA and volcano presentation controls
PCA supports grouping color, grouping shape, three point-size levels, optional sample labels, group encircling, confidence ellipses, ellipse transparency and legend-size control. Default PCA export dimensions are 8 × 7 inches.
The volcano plot defaults to salmon for up-regulated genes, light blue for down-regulated genes and grey for non-significant genes; default point size is 2 and transparency is 0.7. Default volcano PDF dimensions are also 8 × 7 inches.






ImportantThis is not the main proteomics DEP workflow



For normalized protein-abundance data, use Downstream analysis → DEP analysis. The DEG toolkit is built around DESeq2 count modeling and its current code contains a fixed B73-versus-Y12 contrast.








Warning



Do not convert continuous normalized measurements into pseudo-counts merely to make them pass this interface. Statistical model choice should follow the measurement process and data distribution.

title: Stacked Column Diagram
text:
Use Toolkits → Stacked Column Diagram to compare category composition across tissues, samples, treatments, or other groups. The current ProtVis module supports three display modes from the same input table: Stacked columns, Grouped columns, and 100% stacked columns.
This module is useful for summaries such as up/down/not-significant counts, functional-category composition, pathway classes, taxonomic composition, or any other set of numeric categories that should be compared across groups.

title: Stacked Column Diagram
text:
Stacked Column Diagram interface
The screenshot below shows the current ProtVis interface. The left sidebar contains Data Input, Plot Settings, and Download controls. The main area contains the generated Column Chart and a Data Preview panel showing the first eight rows of the current dataset.






Figure 1: ProtVis Stacked Column Diagram interface showing the data-input controls, chart settings, category-color controls, generated column chart and data preview.

title: Stacked Column Diagram
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Load the data. Under Data Input, either upload a tidy .csv file with Upload CSV File or click USE DEMO DATA. ProtVis also provides DOWNLOAD DEMO CSV so the required input structure can be reused as a template.
2. Confirm the input structure. The current implementation requires a column named exactly Tissue. Every other column intended for plotting must be numeric. After loading data, the status box reports the current data source and the Data Preview card shows the first eight rows together with row and column counts.
3. Choose the chart type. Under Plot Settings, select one of the three supported modes:

Stacked columns — category values are stacked and retain their original magnitude.
Grouped columns — categories are displayed side by side within each tissue/group.
100% stacked columns — each column is normalized to the same total height, emphasizing relative composition rather than absolute totals.

4. Adjust the layout. Enable Flip Coordinates when horizontal bars are easier to read. Enable Show Bar Border to draw a black border around each bar segment.
5. Edit labels and typography. Set X-Axis Label, Y-Axis Label, Legend Title, and Base Font Size. The current defaults are Tissue, Count, Category, and a base font size of 12.
6. Set category colors. Once valid data has been loaded, ProtVis creates one color selector for each numeric category column. The category order follows the numeric-column order in the input table, so arrange columns deliberately when a particular legend/stack order is required.
7. Generate the chart. Click RUN CHART. Before the first run, the main panel reports Ready to run; after successful plotting, the status changes to Chart ready and the download button becomes available.
8. Inspect the preview and biological pattern. Check that totals, group order, category order, and relative proportions match the source table. For 100% stacked columns, focus on composition rather than absolute abundance because each group is normalized independently.
9. Export the figure. Under Download, choose PDF, PNG, JPG, or SVG, set width and height in inches, and set DPI for PNG/JPG output. The current defaults are 8 × 6 inches and 300 DPI.

title: Stacked Column Diagram
text:
Input format
The first column must be named Tissue; the remaining plotting columns must be numeric. For example:
Tissue,Down,Not_Significant,Up
Root,120,300,150
Stem,95,280,170
Leaf,140,260,190
Panicle,80,210,130
This is also the structure used by the built-in demonstration dataset.

title: Stacked Column Diagram
text:
How ProtVis constructs the plot
ProtVis keeps Tissue as the grouping variable and converts the remaining numeric category columns from wide format to long format. It then draws the categories with ggplot2::geom_bar(stat = "identity"). The selected chart type determines the position mode: stack, dodge, or fill.
For 100% stacked columns, the plotting layer uses the fill position, so each tissue/group is scaled to the same total height. The underlying numeric values are not replaced in the uploaded dataset; normalization is performed for visualization.

title: Stacked Column Diagram
text:
Choosing the right display
Use Stacked columns when both total magnitude and composition matter. Use Grouped columns when direct category-by-category comparisons are more important than the total. Use 100% stacked columns when comparing relative composition among groups with very different totals.






Tip



If the legend or stack order is biologically important, arrange the numeric category columns in the desired order before upload. ProtVis preserves that column order when constructing the category factor.








Warning



The module currently requires the grouping column to be named exactly Tissue. A differently named first column will not be recognized automatically. Rename the grouping column before upload if necessary.

The current module combines Swiss-Model project information with structure parsing and interactive visualization, so this is the correct tutorial page for the Swiss-Model interface shown below.

title: SwissModel
text:
SwissModel interface
The screenshot below shows a completed Swiss-Model run using the bundled example sequence. ProtVis displays Project Information and Model Quality in the upper result area, while the lower tabs provide PDB Information, Ramachandran Plot, Residue Composition, and an interactive 3D Structure view.






Figure 1: ProtVis SwissModel interface showing sequence input, project information, model-quality results and structure-analysis tabs. The API-token field has been redacted for safe documentation.

title: SwissModel
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Enter the protein sequence. Paste the amino-acid sequence into Protein sequence. Whitespace is removed before submission. The Example button restores the bundled demonstration sequence and is useful for checking that the module is working.
2. Enter a Swiss-Model API token. Supply a valid token in API Token. The token is used to authenticate the modeling request and should be treated as a private credential.
3. Start modeling. Click Run. ProtVis validates that both sequence and token are present, configures the Swiss-Model token, submits the sequence through the automated modeling workflow, waits for the returned project, downloads the predicted structure, and parses the project information.
4. Review Project Information. The Project Information panel reports the returned Swiss-Model project metadata and model records. When a project link is available, open Project Link → Open Swiss-Model result page to inspect the corresponding project on the Swiss-Model website.
5. Review Model Quality. The Model Quality panel summarizes calculated quality information for the downloaded model. Structural interpretation should only proceed after checking the available quality metrics and model coverage.
6. Inspect PDB Information. Open the PDB Information tab to review the parsed structure, including basic atom/residue/chain information from the downloaded model.
7. Inspect the Ramachandran Plot. Use Ramachandran Plot as a stereochemical diagnostic of backbone conformations. Unusual distributions should be interpreted together with model quality and local structural context.
8. Inspect Residue Composition. The Residue Composition tab summarizes the amino-acid composition of the returned structure and provides a quick check of the modeled sequence content.
9. Explore the 3D structure. Open 3D Structure to interactively inspect the predicted protein structure in the embedded r3dmol viewer.
10. Download the outputs. The Download section provides the project information, predicted PDB file, and model-quality table. The current output filenames are swissmodel_project_info.json, swissmodel_model.pdb, and swissmodel_model_quality.csv.

title: SwissModel
text:
Buttons and controls

Run starts the Swiss-Model workflow.
Example restores the built-in protein sequence.
Clear removes the sequence/token inputs and clears current results.
Project Link opens the corresponding Swiss-Model result page after a successful run.
Uploaded / Predicted File Info reports downloaded model-file information.
Download exports project information, the PDB model, and model-quality results.

title: SwissModel
text:
Interpretation
A successful modeling job does not by itself establish that every region of the model is reliable. Review the available quality metrics, model coverage, stereochemical diagnostics, and any unsupported or poorly modeled regions before mapping mutations, PTMs, domains, or functional residues.
When the structure is used in a figure or manuscript, record the Swiss-Model project/model identifier and preserve the downloaded PDB and model-quality outputs so that the structural interpretation remains traceable.






ImportantKeep API tokens private



Do not publish API tokens in screenshots, manuscripts, repositories, notebooks, or exported project files. The token field in the documentation screenshot has therefore been redacted.








Warning



Predicted structures and experimentally determined structures are not equivalent evidence. Report the prediction source and relevant model-quality information, and avoid strong mechanistic claims for poorly supported regions without additional evidence.

title: Protein extract
text:
Use Toolkits → Protein extract when you have a reference protein FASTA and a list of candidate gene/protein IDs and need the corresponding sequences for structure prediction, primer/tag design, domain analysis or other downstream work.
The current ProtVis matcher is not limited to literal header equality. It first attempts an exact header-token match, then a normalized stable-ID match, and finally allows a unique one-character fuzzy match under restricted conditions. This makes the module useful for FASTA files whose headers contain transcript/protein isoform suffixes.

title: Protein extract
text:
Protein Extraction interface
The screenshot below shows a maize reference FASTA with four queried stable IDs. The example FASTA contains 72,539 entries, and one stable query can match multiple FASTA isoforms, which is why the displayed number of matched FASTA sequences can be larger than the number of queried IDs.






Figure 1: ProtVis Protein Extraction interface showing FASTA upload, manual protein-ID input, extraction summary metrics and matched FASTA sequences.

title: Protein extract
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Upload the reference protein FASTA. Supported inputs include .fa, .faa, .fasta, and their gzip-compressed forms such as .fa.gz, .faa.gz, and .fasta.gz.
2. Choose the Protein ID Input Method. Select Manual Input to paste one ID per line, or File Upload to provide a .txt, .csv, or .tsv ID list. For CSV/TSV inputs, ProtVis reads all non-empty values as candidate identifiers, so keep unrelated metadata out of the file.
3. Review the query IDs. Remove accidental duplicates and blank lines. Stable gene IDs are often preferable when the goal is to retrieve all corresponding protein/transcript isoforms; isoform-specific IDs are appropriate when only one record is intended.
4. Click Run Extraction. ProtVis parses the FASTA headers, matches the requested IDs and enables Download Results when at least one FASTA sequence has been recovered.
5. Check the three summary metrics. Total FASTA Entries is the number of sequences in the reference FASTA. Queried IDs is the number of unique input IDs. The current UI label Matched IDs counts matched FASTA sequence entries, not necessarily unique input IDs; therefore it can exceed Queried IDs when one stable query maps to several isoforms.
6. Review Matched Summary. Use this tab to confirm which input IDs were found and how they were matched. Do not assume that every returned isoform is biologically equivalent; the FASTA annotation determines which protein records are associated with a stable gene/transcript identifier.
7. Inspect Sequence Table and FASTA Viewer. Sequence Table provides structured sequence information, while FASTA Viewer shows the matched records in FASTA format. In the screenshot, several records from the same maize stable ID are visible because the reference contains multiple protein/transcript isoforms.
8. Check Unmatched IDs. This tab should always be reviewed before downstream analysis. An unmatched candidate may indicate a database-version mismatch, an unexpected header convention, a genuinely absent sequence, or a query too different to satisfy the controlled fuzzy-matching rule.
9. Download the result package. Download Results generates protein_extract_results_YYYY-MM-DD.zip. The ZIP contains matched_sequences.fasta, summary.txt, and unmatched_ids.txt.

title: Protein extract
text:
How ID matching works
ProtVis searches FASTA header tokens using three stages. First, it tries an exact case-insensitive token match. If that fails, it compares normalized stable IDs. Normalization removes common gene:, transcript:, or protein: prefixes, leading >, trailing descriptive text, common protein/transcript/isoform suffixes such as _P001, _T002, -isoform1, and terminal numeric version suffixes.
If neither exact nor normalized matching succeeds, ProtVis can use a one-character fuzzy match only when the canonical query is at least eight characters long and the approximate comparison identifies a single stable ID. This last restriction reduces the risk of silently selecting one of several equally plausible near matches.






WarningInspect multi-isoform matches



A stable gene ID can legitimately return multiple FASTA entries. The summary metric therefore reflects matched sequence records rather than a strict one-query/one-sequence relationship. Use the Sequence Table and FASTA headers to decide which isoform is appropriate for downstream work.








Tip



Keep the unmatched_ids.txt file even when only a few queries fail. It is a useful record for diagnosing reference-version and identifier-conversion problems later.

title: Correct noise
text:
Correct Noise is the first source-independent preprocessing module. It loads the active ProtVis_dataset whenever possible, shows the expression matrix and sample information, optionally normalizes sample-column names, and applies the replicate-aware correction rule.
The interface has three principal actions: Load data, Rename Columns, and Correct Noise.

title: Correct noise
text:
Correct Noise is the first source-independent preprocessing module. It loads the active ProtVis_dataset whenever possible, shows the expression matrix and sample information, optionally normalizes sample-column names, and applies the replicate-aware correction rule.
The interface has three principal actions: Load data, Rename Columns, and Correct Noise.

title: Correct noise
Correct noise
text:
Replicate-aware correction rule
For datasets that use replicate suffixes _1, _2, and _3, ProtVis groups corresponding replicate columns and evaluates each protein within that group.

If at least two replicate measurements are non-zero, zero/missing cells are replaced using half of the sum of the non-zero replicate values.
If fewer than two non-zero replicates are present, the replicate-group values are set to zero and then converted to NA.
If no recognizable replicate suffixes exist, ProtVis returns the validated matrix without applying replicate-level correction.
Duplicate protein IDs are collapsed before the correction step, retaining the largest finite intensity per sample, to prevent many-to-many joins or reshaping from expanding the table.







Note



This behavior is intentionally different from a generic “more than half missing” filter or mean imputation. Missing-value imputation remains a separate downstream stage.

title: Correct noise
text:
GUI workflow
The screenshot below shows the actual Correct Noise interface for the Sage-derived PXD065315 example. The red labels identify the recommended order.






Figure 1: Correct Noise in ProtVis. Marker 1 loads the completed input/search result, marker 2 renames or validates sample columns, and marker 3 runs replicate-aware noise correction. The main panel provides Sample info, Expression Matrix, Rename Columns and Correct Noise result tabs.



Follow the numbered controls. 1. Load data. Open Pre-processing → Correct Noise and click Load data. Wait for the green Data loaded status, then inspect Sample info and Expression Matrix. Check that the expected sample columns are present and that the protein table is non-empty. The 5,209 rows visible in the screenshot are specific to this example run and are not a required target count for other datasets.
2. Rename Columns. Click Rename Columns. ProtVis uses maxquant_id mappings when they are available; otherwise already-valid sample_id names are retained. Inspect the Rename Columns result before continuing. For the illustrated Raw/Sage project, the intended columns are B73_C1, B73_C2, B73_C3, EA2024_C1, EA2024_C2, and EA2024_C3. Unexpected duplicate or unmatched sample names should be fixed before correction because replicate grouping depends on stable identifiers.
3. Correct Noise. Click Correct Noise. After a successful run, ProtVis switches to the Correct Noise result tab automatically. Compare the corrected table with the loaded expression matrix and verify that protein IDs, sample names, row count, zero values and newly introduced NA values are biologically and technically plausible.
Long-running actions use duplicate-run guards. A second rapid click on Load, Rename, or Correct Noise while the same operation is already running is ignored rather than executing it twice.

title: Correct noise
text:
Outputs
The corrected matrix is written back into a new traceable ProtVis_dataset analysis state. ProtVis records the noise_correction result and process entry with the method replicate_correction.
For compatibility and recovery, the current implementation writes both:
Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda
Step3_correct_noise.rda
Step2 is refreshed as the cross-source handoff, while Step3 remains the downstream compatibility snapshot.
Continue with Data transformation.

title: Correct noise
text:
Troubleshooting
“No completed input stage was found.” Finish the previous input route first: run Sage Search for Raw data, MaxQuant Output Preparation for MaxQuant, or the appropriate parser/import for another source.
“The current ProtVis_dataset has no expression matrix.” The object is most likely a Raw/Sage staging project. Complete Search so Sage LFQ can create the protein matrix.
The corrected table looks empty although the action succeeded. Current ProtVis automatically selects the Correct Noise result tab after completion. If an older installation still behaves differently, reinstall the current dev version.
Working-directory errors after a restart. The module resolves the project directory from the shared workdir, dataset metadata, checkpoint metadata, Raw input directory, and finally the current R working directory. Keeping the project directory intact makes recovery more reliable.

title: Data imputation
text:
Proteomics missingness can arise from abundance limits, identification uncertainty, stochastic sampling, or technical failures. ProtVis therefore keeps missing values explicit until the user chooses an imputation method.
Before imputation, the current module coerces quantitative columns to numeric, converts non-finite values to missing, and handles not-observed sentinels such as 0 and -8 as NA. Rows or columns that are entirely missing are removed from the matrix used by the imputation calculation.

title: Data imputation
text:
Available methods
The current GUI provides:







Method
Typical use




kNN
Local similarity-based imputation; current default


RF
Random-forest based imputation


Mean
Column mean replacement; useful mainly as a simple baseline


Median
Column median replacement


Zero

title: Data imputation
text:
GUI workflow
The screenshot below shows the full Data Imputation interface and the recommended operating order.






Figure 1: Data Imputation in ProtVis. Numbered controls guide the user from loading transformed data, visualizing missing values, choosing an imputation method, reviewing the q for MinProb compatibility field, and running imputation. The main panel compares original and imputed data and their missing-value visualizations.



Follow the numbered controls in the screenshot. 1. Load data. Click Load data to load the transformed ProtVis_dataset or its Step4 compatibility state. Confirm the green Data loaded status, then check the Sample Info and Expression Matrix tabs before changing any missing values.
2. Visualize missing values. Click Visualize missing values. ProtVis opens the diagnostic view containing Original Data and Original Data Visualization. Inspect whether missingness is concentrated in particular proteins or samples. If a sample is almost entirely missing, investigate the input/search/QC problem before attempting to solve it by imputation.
3. Select the imputation Method. Expand Imputation Settings and choose kNN, RF, Mean, Median, Zero, or Minimum. kNN is selected by default, but the default is not automatically the correct method for every proteomics experiment. ProtVis warns when rows with more than 50% missing values are present because similarity-based kNN estimates can become unstable for those rows.
4. Interpret q for MinProb correctly. The current interface still displays a numeric q for MinProb control (0.01 in the screenshot) for compatibility with earlier UI designs. In the present implementation, however, the active method menu does not contain a MinProb method and the current kNN, RF, Mean, Median, Zero, and Minimum branches do not use this q value. Do not report the q field as an active parameter unless a future ProtVis version restores a MinProb method.
5. Run imputation. Click Run imputation. After completion, compare Imputed Data and Imputed Data Visualization with the original panels. Confirm that missing cells were handled as intended and that the result did not create implausible sample distributions. Use the Download section to export the original and imputed diagnostic plots when they are needed for the analysis record.






ImportantDefault does not mean universally correct



kNN is the interface default, but no imputation method is optimal for every missingness mechanism. Report the method actually selected in the Methods section and preserve the pre-imputation project state for auditability.

title: Data imputation
text:
Output
The imputed matrix is written into the active ProtVis_dataset, recorded in the analysis/process history, and persisted in:
Step5_data_imputation.rda
Continue with Data normalization.

title: DEP analysis
text: The current DEP module uses limma (lmFit, contrasts, eBayes, topTable) on the normalized protein-abundance matrix. Each row of the comparison table defines a Group1 versus Group2 contrast.

title: DEP analysis
text: The current DEP module uses limma (lmFit, contrasts, eBayes, topTable) on the normalized protein-abundance matrix. Each row of the comparison table defines a Group1 versus Group2 contrast.

title: DEP analysis
text:
DEP interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current DEP page with an active B73 vs EA2024 comparison. It includes the data preview, comparison setup, DEP table, volcano plot, heatmap and DEP-count summary in one interface.






Figure 1: ProtVis differential protein abundance interface. The page shows Load Data, Sample Info and Normalized Data previews, a B73 versus EA2024 comparison, DEP table, volcano plot, heatmap, DEP-count bar chart, comparison controls and the Run DEP action.




Recommended operating order
1. Load the normalized project data. Open Downstream analysis → DEP analysis and click LOAD DATA. Confirm that the status reaches completion, then inspect Sample Info and Normalized Data. Do not start a contrast until sample identifiers, grouping metadata and the normalized matrix are aligned.
2. Define the group comparison. ProtVis accepts a comparison table with exactly two columns, Group1 and Group2. You can use the built-in/demo comparison, edit or paste a comparison table, or upload a .csv/.xlsx file. In the screenshot, the active contrast is B73 vs EA2024. Group labels must exactly match the values used in the relevant sample_info grouping field.
A minimal comparison file is:
Group1,Group2
B73,EA2024
Multiple rows can be supplied when several contrasts are required. ProtVis processes each valid row and creates a separate result view for each comparison.
3. Set the significance/display thresholds. The current volcano controls start with logFC threshold = 0.27, corresponding to about a 1.21-fold change on a log2 scale, and P-value threshold = 0.05. These controls determine the displayed Upregulated, Downregulated and Not significant classes. Changing the thresholds updates the reactive plots; it does not recompute the underlying limma model.
4. Click RUN DEP. Start the analysis only after the comparison table and thresholds are sensible. Follow the DEP Analysis Progress indicator until the run completes. Long-running actions are protected against rapid duplicate clicks in the current ProtVis interface.
5. Inspect the DEP table before the plots. The result table contains logFC, average expression and limma significance statistics. Use the table as the quantitative record and export it with the available copy/CSV/Excel controls when needed.
6. Interpret the volcano, heatmap and DEP-count plot together. The volcano plot summarizes effect size and significance, the heatmap shows the abundance pattern of the currently significant protein set, and the DEP-count plot summarizes the number of classified proteins. In the screenshot these views are synchronized for B73 vs EA2024.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Prepare comparisons
ProtVis accepts a comparison table with exactly two columns:
Group1,Group2
Control,Treatment
Root,Shoot
The group labels must exactly match values in the relevant sample_info grouping column. A mismatch in spelling, capitalization, or whitespace can produce an invalid contrast even when the biological groups are conceptually the same.
The interface also supports built-in/demo comparisons derived from available metadata as well as user-supplied CompareGroup files. Use the comparison source that corresponds to the actual experimental factor being tested.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Current significance controls
The volcano panel currently starts with:

logFC threshold = 0.27 (approximately a 1.21-fold change on a log2 scale);
P-value threshold = 0.05.

The displayed regulation classification uses logFC together with the raw limma P.Value. The limma result table also contains multiple-testing-adjusted statistics.






ImportantUse adjusted p-values for publication-grade FDR control



If the analysis plan requires FDR control, base final biological claims and downstream ID lists on the adjusted p-value column, such as adj.P.Val, rather than assuming the volcano panel’s raw P.Value cutoff is an FDR threshold. Record both the effect-size and significance thresholds used in the manuscript Methods.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Dynamic plots
Volcano thresholds are reactive: changing them reclassifies proteins and keeps the DEP heatmap synchronized with the currently significant set. Heatmaps sanitize non-finite values only for plotting; this does not rewrite the differential-statistics table.
A useful review order is therefore table → volcano → heatmap → DEP count, because the table preserves the complete model output while the plots are filtered visual summaries.

title: DEP analysis
text:
Output and downstream handoff
DEP results are attached to the active project object and are available to Enrichment analysis. The current enrichment loader checks the project object first and can also recover differential results from:
Step7_differential_analysis.rda
with older filenames retained only as migration fallbacks.
After validating the comparison and significant-protein list, continue to the functional-analysis modules such as Enrichment analysis, GSEA, or Pathview.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Use Downstream analysis → Overview after preprocessing and before differential abundance analysis. It is the fastest place to check sample relationships, normalization effects, missingness, replicate behavior and broad data quality before formal testing.
The current module loads both the imputed and normalized stages. When stage snapshots are unavailable but a valid ProtVis_dataset is active, ProtVis can derive an overview from the current project object and report that fallback.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Overview interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current Overview/QC page using the six-sample maize example. Values such as 5,209 proteins and 6 samples belong to this example and should not be treated as fixed ProtVis output sizes.






Figure 1: ProtVis Overview and quality-control interface. The left panel begins with Load Data and provides Correlation, Expression pattern and Dimensionality Reduction controls. The main area compares dimensionality-reduction results before and after normalization and summarizes proteomics QC, missingness and sample-level intensity diagnostics.




Recommended operating order
1. Load the project data. Open Downstream analysis → Overview and click Load Data. ProtVis loads the imputed and normalized quantitative states needed for side-by-side diagnostics. Confirm the status message before interpreting any plot. In the screenshot, both datasets load successfully and each contains 5,209 proteins across 6 samples.
2. Inspect correlation first. Open Correlation, choose Pearson, Spearman, or Kendall, and inspect whether samples expected to be biologically similar cluster together. Correlation is especially useful for identifying a single failed replicate or a sample whose overall profile is inconsistent with its group.
3. Inspect the expression-pattern heatmap. Use Expression pattern to view broad abundance structure among the most variable proteins. This view is intended for global pattern checking rather than formal differential-abundance inference. If scaling is enabled, interpret relative patterns rather than absolute abundance differences.
4. Compare dimensionality reduction before and after normalization. In Dimensionality Reduction, choose PCA, PCoA, t-SNE, UMAP, or NMDS. The screenshot uses UMAP and displays results before normalization and after normalization side by side. A useful normalization should reduce unwanted technical structure without erasing biologically plausible separation.
5. Set grouping aesthetics from sample metadata. Color and 95% confidence ellipses can use metadata such as group, tissue, species, batch, or condition; point shape can be assigned independently. In the illustrated interface, tissue is used for color/ellipse grouping and species for point shape. Use fields that match the actual experimental design rather than forcing the demo defaults onto another dataset.
6. Finish with the proteomics QC panel. Review the Proteomics QC summary, missing-value rate by sample, sample total normalized intensity, intensity distributions, PCA/CV diagnostics and related summaries. Unexpectedly high missingness, a large sample-level intensity shift, or a single isolated sample should be investigated before DEP analysis.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Correlation
Choose Pearson, Spearman, or Kendall correlation, then configure clustering and whether correlation values/sample names are displayed. Replicates do not need to be identical, but samples from the same biological condition should usually be more similar to one another than to unrelated groups unless the experiment provides a biological reason otherwise.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Expression pattern
The expression-pattern heatmap can focus on the top variable features and optionally scale by protein or sample. This is useful for identifying broad coordinated patterns, outlier samples and dominant abundance blocks. It should not replace a statistical DEP model.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Dimensionality reduction
Available methods are:

PCA
PCoA
t-SNE
UMAP
NMDS

ProtVis displays dimensionality reduction before normalization and after normalization so that the effect of preprocessing can be assessed directly. For stochastic methods such as t-SNE or UMAP, interpret neighborhood structure together with the experimental design rather than treating axis values as directly comparable biological quantities.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Proteomics QC
The QC panel summarizes and exports key diagnostics including sample total intensity, sample missing-value rate, intensity boxplots/density, PCA based on variable features, coefficient-of-variation distributions and the normalized matrix.






WarningDo not select a preprocessing strategy only because a plot looks cleaner



A visually tighter PCA or UMAP is not proof that preprocessing is correct. If normalization creates separation that conflicts with known biology, removes a strong expected effect, or produces implausible sample distributions, return to the preceding preprocessing stages and check the assumptions.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Handoff to DEP analysis
Once sample relationships, missingness, distributions and group structure are acceptable, continue to DEP analysis. Keep the Overview/QC outputs as part of the analysis record because they provide the context needed to judge the reliability of downstream differential results.

Recommended installation

  CRAN = "https://mirrors.tuna.tsinghua.edu.cn/CRAN/"
))

packageVersion("ProtVis")
# 0.7.9 for the cookbook baseline
Because dev changes continuously, a later installation may report a newer version. In that case, prefer the current ProtVis source and Help page when a control or default differs from this cookbook.

title: Installation
text:
Clean update
When an old installation is stale, locked, or its lazy-load database is corrupted, use the clean installer supplied by ProtVis:
source(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xuebinzhang-lab/ProtVis/dev/install_ProtVis.R"
)
Close other R sessions that are currently using ProtVis before running a clean reinstall.

title: Installation
text:
Sage availability
Raw/mzML projects can run a Sage database search from the conditional Search tab.
On Windows, ProtVis first looks for its bundled executable at inst/extdata/sage/windows/sage.exe. On Linux or macOS, install Sage separately and make the sage executable available on PATH. You can verify discovery from R with:
ProtVis::protvis_sage_executable()
A valid path means the search engine is available. NULL means ProtVis could not locate Sage.

title: Installation
text:
Optional WGCNA helper
Some WGCNA workflows may use the optional helper package documented by ProtVis:
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ShawnWx2019/WGCNAShinyFun", ref = "master")
You do not need this optional dependency to launch the core application.

title: Installation
text:
Launch ProtVis
library(ProtVis)
run_ProtVis()
or directly:
ProtVis::run_ProtVis()

title: Installation
text:
First launch checklist
After the application opens, confirm that you can see Homepage, Project init, Pre-processing, Downstream analysis, Multi-omics, PTM, Release data, Toolkits, and Help.
Two navigation items are intentionally conditional:

Search is shown when Raw is selected in Project init.
Pre-processing → MaxQuant Output Preparation is shown only when MaxQuant is selected.

The source-independent preprocessing items, including Correct Noise, remain available for all supported data sources.
If the app opens but an optional module reports a missing dependency, install that dependency and restart the R session. If the package itself fails to load after an update, prefer the clean installer above rather than repeatedly installing over a corrupted package directory.

title: Project init
text:
Project init establishes the analysis context shared by all later modules. It defines the writable project directory, sample metadata, data source, and—when already available—the quantitative expression matrix. It then creates the first validated ProtVis_dataset and saves the initial project stage.
The current interface supports two distinct starting patterns:

Tabular quantitative data: sample metadata + an expression matrix or a built-in source example.
Raw/mzML + Sage: sample metadata + mzML directory + protein FASTA. In this route, Project init can create a valid Sage staging object before an expression matrix exists.

title: Project init
text:
Common inputs
Sample information can be uploaded as .csv, .xlsx, or .xls. A practical table contains a unique sample identifier and the grouping variables required later in the analysis.







Column
Purpose




sample_id
Unique sample name used by downstream matrices and plots


maxquant_id
Original source/export name used when sample columns must be mapped or renamed


group
Experimental group used for comparisons


tissue
Optional biological tissue; used by several demo and dimensionality-reduction workflows


species or organism
Optional biological source metadata


batch
Optional batch grouping


condition
Optional condition grouping


mzml_file
Required for the Raw/Sage route; exact mzML filename corresponding to the sample



For an ordinary tabular project, the expression matrix should contain a protein identifier plus numeric sample columns. Sample columns must be unambiguously alignable to sample_info.

title: Project init
text:
Supported source selections
The Project init source menu currently includes Raw, MaxQuant, ProteomeDiscoverer / Proteome Discoverer, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe, Skyline, Mascot, OpenMS, and User-defined matrix. Raw is the current default selection.
Navigation is source-aware. The top-level Search tab is shown only for Raw. Pre-processing → MaxQuant Output Preparation is shown only for MaxQuant. The remaining preprocessing modules stay available across sources.

title: Project init
text:
Standard tabular workflow

Click Set working directory and choose a writable project directory.
Upload Sample Information.
Upload the Expression Matrix, or choose a Built-in example and click Load selected built-in example.
Select the matching Data source.
Confirm the Sample Info and Expression Matrix previews.
Click Project init.

ProtVis validates sample/matrix alignment, creates ProtVis_dataset, performs an automatic portable export, and saves Step1_project_init.rda.

title: Project init
text:
Raw/mzML + Sage workflow
Choose this route when the starting material is converted mass-spectrometry data in mzML format and you want ProtVis to run the Sage database search. The full-resolution screenshot below is the original PNG uploaded from the running application; the red labels show the required operating order.






Figure 1: Raw/mzML Project init workflow in ProtVis. The red labels indicate the recommended order: 1 set working directory, 2 upload sample information, 3 upload protein FASTA, 4 select the mzML input directory, 5 check mzML files, 6 select Raw as the data source, and 7 run Project init. The right panel shows the six PXD065315 control samples after successful initialization.




Follow the numbered order in the figure
1. Set the working directory. Click Set working directory and choose a local directory in which ProtVis can create stage files, portable exports, the Sage_search directory and later analysis outputs. The illustrated project uses E:/count/p_raw. The directory must exist and be writable. Keeping one analysis inside a stable project directory makes checkpoint and Sage-result recovery much more reliable.
2. Load the sample information. Upload a .csv, .xlsx, or .xls table with at least sample_id and mzml_file, or click Use built-in PXD065315 sample information for the six-sample maize control example. Wait for Upload complete, then inspect the Sample Info preview. For the built-in example, the six rows are B73_C1, B73_C2, B73_C3, EA2024_C1, EA2024_C2, and EA2024_C3; the mzml_file field must point to the corresponding .mzML names.
3. Upload the protein FASTA. Under Raw/mzML input, upload the protein database used for Sage. Accepted inputs include .fa, .fasta, .faa, and supported compressed FASTA forms. Use a FASTA that matches the organism and protein identifiers expected for the experiment. In the illustrated maize example, UP000007305_4577.fasta is registered. Do not continue until the interface reports FASTA ready.
4. Select the mzML input directory. Click Select mzML input directory and choose the folder containing the converted mzML files. The folder may also contain the original vendor .raw files, but the check is performed against the .mzML filenames registered in sample_info. For PXD065315, the expected converted files are B73_C1.mzML, B73_C2.mzML, B73_C3.mzML, EA2024_C1.mzML, EA2024_C2.mzML, and EA2024_C3.mzML.
5. Check the mzML files. Click Check mzML files. ProtVis verifies that filenames are unique, have the .mzML extension and exist in the selected directory. Resolve every Missing or Invalid extension row before initializing the project. If a check fails, compare the physical filename with sample_info$mzml_file character by character.
6. Select Raw as the data source. In Select data source, choose Raw. This activates the Raw/Sage route and exposes the top-level Search tab. Do not upload a fabricated expression matrix merely to satisfy Project init; the expression layer is deliberately absent until Sage produces LFQ results.
7. Run Project init. Click the large Project init button. A successful Raw initialization reports “PROJECT INIT completed — Sage ProtVis_dataset is ready.” Inspect the preview tabs after completion. Sample Info should contain the expected rows, Raw/mzML Files should reflect the registered files, and Expression Matrix can remain empty at this stage. The next step is Search, not Correct Noise.
When an uploaded sample table contains an mzML filename column (mzml_file, mzml, raw_file, file, or filename), ProtVis automatically registers it for the Sage workflow.






ImportantDo not create a fake expression matrix



A Raw/Sage project does not need a protein expression matrix before Search. Project init creates a Sage_staging project object and fills the expression layer only after LFQ results are available. After Step 7 succeeds, continue directly to Raw/mzML + Sage search.




The Sage staging object
If no expression matrix exists yet, Project init creates a staging ProtVis_dataset with sample metadata and registered input paths. Its workflow stage is Sage_staging, with an object name such as:
ProtVis_dataset__project_init__Sage_staging__v1
This is intentional. ProtVis does not fabricate protein abundances before the database search. The staging object is valid even though its expression layer is temporarily empty. Step1_project_init.rda and the portable export are still written, so the project has a recoverable starting state.

title: Project init
text:
Built-in PXD065315 sample information
The current built-in Raw example contains six maize control samples: three B73 replicates (B73_C1, B73_C2, B73_C3) and three EA2024 replicates (EA2024_C1, EA2024_C2, EA2024_C3). Its columns include sample_id, mzml_file, genotype, treatment, group, condition, replicate, batch, tissue, organism, accession, and the PRIDE source URL.
Public source data:

The built-in mzml_file values refer to locally converted files such as B73_C1.mzML and EA2024_C3.mzML. PRIDE provides the corresponding vendor .raw files; convert them to mzML before selecting the Raw/mzML directory in ProtVis.

title: Project init
text:
Outputs
For a standard quantitative project, the primary output is a validated ProtVis_dataset with a traceable name such as:
ProtVis_dataset__project_init__maxquant__v1
For either starting route, ProtVis writes:
Step1_project_init.rda
The stage file contains one ProtVis_dataset, rather than separate unrelated workspace variables.






TipVerify the route before clicking Project init



For Raw/Sage, check mzML files and FASTA registration first. For a tabular project, inspect the sample and expression previews. This catches filename, sample-order and working-directory problems before downstream steps begin.

title: Project init
text:
Common validation problems
Raw project creates no expression preview. This is expected before Sage Search. The staging object intentionally has no protein abundance matrix.
mzML check reports Missing. The mzml_file values must match the files in the selected directory. The check is case-aware at the filesystem level and also rejects non-mzML extensions or duplicate names.
Sample names do not match a tabular matrix. Check sample_id, maxquant_id, and expression-matrix column names. Do not silently reorder samples outside ProtVis without recording the change.
Working directory cannot be selected. Choose a local directory you can write to. ProtVis normalizes selected paths and rejects inaccessible locations instead of continuing with an invalid project directory.

title: PTM analysis
text:
The PTM section is intended for modification-centric proteomics workflows in which peptide/site-level evidence needs to be inspected separately from ordinary protein abundance analysis.
Because PTM search-engine exports differ substantially in site localization, peptide sequence, modification notation and protein mapping, always check that the selected source parser and input columns match the dataset that generated the evidence.

title: PTM analysis
text:
Recommended workflow

Complete the standard project setup and source selection.
Open PTM and load the PTM-specific table expected by the module.
Verify modified sequence/site notation and protein identifiers before filtering.
Apply localization/evidence filters appropriate to the experiment.
Inspect modification-level quantitative patterns separately from total protein abundance.
Export the filtered evidence table used for every figure.

title: PTM analysis
text:
Biological interpretation
A change at a phosphosite, acetylation site or other PTM can reflect altered modification occupancy, altered total protein abundance, or both. When possible, compare PTM abundance with the corresponding protein-level signal before assigning a regulatory interpretation.






Warning



Do not interpret a modified peptide as a unique site when the search result does not localize the modification confidently. Preserve the original localization evidence in the exported record.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Use Multi-omics → Co-enrichment after enrichment analysis has been completed separately for multiple omics layers, contrasts, tissues, or protein clusters. The module compares enrichment results across two or three omics datasets, identifies shared and omics-specific pathways, and provides publication-oriented summary tables and plots.
The most important requirement is comparability: enrichment results should use compatible pathway identifiers, annotation versions, and biological backgrounds. A pathway appearing in only one layer can reflect true biology, but it can also arise from incompatible annotation systems or different background universes.
